lessons.title: Wet Waste, Dry Waste
objectives: Sort waste into wet (kitchen) and dry
Explain why we use bins
explanation: Waste is what we throw away. Wet waste comes from the kitchen: fruit peels, vegetable scraps and leftover food. It can rot and become compost.
Dry waste includes paper, plastic, glass and metal. Much of it can be recycled into new things.
Putting waste in the right bin keeps our homes and streets clean and helps recycling. Litter on the ground can hurt animals and block drains.

story.title: The Two Bins
story.text: Momo had a green bin and a blue bin. Kiko threw a banana peel and a juice box in the same bin. "Oops!" said Momo, "The peel goes in green — it turns into compost. The box goes in blue — it can be recycled." Kiko sorted them, and the bins smiled.

Cloth bags can be used hundreds of times instead of plastic bags. Old clothes can be passed to younger cousins or friends.
Every time we reuse something, we save the trees, water and energy needed to make a new one.

lessons.title: The Three Rs
objectives: Explain reduce, reuse and recycle
Put the 3 Rs in order of best to good
explanation: Reduce means making less waste in the first place — like carrying a water bottle instead of buying plastic ones, or saying no to things we don't need.
Reuse means using things again. Recycle means turning old materials into new things: old paper into new paper, glass bottles into new bottles, aluminium cans into new cans.
Reduce is best, then reuse, then recycle. Recycling is good but still uses energy and water.

lessons.title: Switch It Off!
objectives: Name ways to save electricity
Explain where electricity comes from in simple terms
explanation: Lights, fans, TVs and fridges all use electricity. Much of India's electricity is made in power stations that burn coal, which pollutes the air.
We can save electricity by switching off lights and fans when leaving a room, using daylight, and switching off devices at the plug when not in use.
Saving electricity saves money and helps the air stay cleaner.

lessons.title: Plastic Lasts Forever (Almost)
objectives: Explain why plastic pollution is harmful
Suggest alternatives to single-use plastic
explanation: Plastic is strong, light and cheap — that's why it's everywhere. But most plastic doesn't rot. A plastic bottle can last for hundreds of years, breaking into tiny pieces called microplastics.
Plastic litter can block drains, causing floods, and harm animals. Cows on streets may eat plastic bags; sea turtles may mistake bags for jellyfish.
Single-use plastics — used once then thrown away — are the biggest problem. Alternatives include cloth bags, steel bottles and tiffins, and traditional leaf plates (pattals).

lessons.title: Hug a Tree: The Chipko Story
objectives: List benefits of trees
Retell the Chipko movement and explain its importance
explanation: Trees give us oxygen, shade, fruit, wood and medicines. Their roots hold soil in place so it doesn't wash away. They are homes for birds, insects and animals.

In the 1970s, in the hills of Uttarakhand, villagers — many of them women — protected their forests by hugging trees so that contractors could not cut them. This was the Chipko movement ("chipko" means "to cling").
Chipko inspired forest protection across India. Today we can help by planting native trees and caring for them until they are strong.

context.text: A well-known Chipko action took place at Reni village in 1974, where Gaura Devi led women in protecting the forest. Sunderlal Bahuguna and Chandi Prasad Bhatt were among its prominent leaders.
In 1730, according to tradition, Amrita Devi Bishnoi and many others of the Bishnoi community gave their lives to protect khejri trees at Khejarli, Rajasthan.

vocabulary.meaning: a forest protection movement where people hugged trees

examples: Neem, peepal and banyan are native trees in much of India.

story.title: The Women of Reni
story.text: In 1974, when men from the village were away, contractors arrived to cut trees near Reni. Gaura Devi and the village women went into the forest and stood with their arms around the trees. "This forest is our mother's home," they said. The contractors left, and the forest stood.

lessons.title: Sun, Wind and Water Power
objectives: Distinguish renewable and non-renewable energy
Evaluate advantages and limitations of each
explanation: Non-renewable energy comes from fossil fuels — coal, oil and natural gas — formed over millions of years. They will run out, and burning them releases carbon dioxide and air pollution.
Renewable energy comes from sources that are naturally replenished: solar (sunlight), wind, hydroelectric (flowing water) and biogas (from animal dung and food waste).

Renewables have challenges: the Sun doesn't shine at night and wind isn't constant, so storage (batteries) and planning are needed. India has rapidly expanded solar power, including large solar parks in Rajasthan and Karnataka.

story.title: The Solar Village

lessons.title: Measuring My Footprint
objectives: Explain what a carbon footprint is
Identify the biggest parts of a household footprint and ways to reduce them
explanation: A carbon footprint is the total greenhouse gases released by our activities — travel, electricity, food and the things we buy.

Typically, big parts include transport (cars and flights), electricity from fossil fuels, and food (especially meat and food waste). Walking, cycling, public transport, saving electricity and wasting less food all help.
Footprints vary hugely between people and countries. People in some wealthy countries have footprints many times larger than the average person in India. Fairness is part of the climate conversation.

examples: Cycling to school instead of being driven reduces emissions.

lessons.title: The 17 Global Goals
objectives: Define sustainable development
Explain links between several SDGs
explanation: Sustainable development means "development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs" (Brundtland Report, 1987).

In 2015, United Nations member states agreed 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) for 2030, including no poverty, zero hunger, quality education, clean water, affordable clean energy, climate action and life on land and below water.
The goals are connected: clean energy can improve health (less smoke from cooking fires), education can reduce poverty, and protecting forests helps climate and livelihoods.

story.title: The Smoke-Free Kitchen
story.text: In many villages, women cooked on wood fires, breathing smoke every day. Clean cooking gas programmes reduced the smoke, improving health (SDG 3), saving time for women and girls (SDG 5), and reducing tree cutting (SDG 15). "One change," said the health worker, "helps many goals."

lessons.title: From Take-Make-Waste to Circular
objectives: Compare linear and circular economies
Evaluate the role of informal recyclers in India
explanation: A linear economy follows "take, make, waste": extract resources, make products, throw them away. A circular economy keeps materials in use: design for durability, repair, reuse, remanufacture and recycle, so waste is minimised.
Extended producer responsibility (EPR) makes companies responsible for collecting and recycling their packaging and products after use. India has EPR rules for plastic packaging and electronic waste.

In India, a large informal workforce of waste pickers and kabadiwalas collects and sorts recyclables, recovering a significant share of materials, often in difficult and unsafe conditions. Recognising and protecting these workers is part of a fair circular economy.

vocabulary.meaning: a system that keeps materials in use and minimises waste
take, make, waste
making producers responsible for their products' end of life
a local scrap dealer who buys recyclables

examples: Repair cafés help people fix appliances instead of discarding them.
Refillable detergent stations reduce packaging.

story.title: The Kabadiwala's Bicycle
story.text: Every Sunday, the kabadiwala cycled down Zuri's street calling "Raddi!" He bought old newspapers, bottles and metal, sorted them, and sold them to recyclers. Zuri realised he was part of a giant recycling system — keeping materials in use long before the word "circular economy" was popular.

lessons.title: Why Value Nature?
objectives: Compare different ethical views of nature
Analyse environmental justice issues
explanation: Anthropocentrism values nature mainly for its usefulness to humans. Biocentrism values all living things for their own sake. Ecocentrism values whole ecosystems, including rivers and mountains.
Environmental justice asks who bears the costs of pollution and who receives the benefits. Often poorer communities live closest to polluting industries or waste dumps.

Many traditions express reverence for nature — sacred groves, Bishnoi protection of wildlife, Jain ahimsa, Indigenous land stewardship. These can inform ethics alongside scientific evidence and democratic debate.

context.text: Philosophers and communities disagree about the basis of our duties to nature; these positions are presented for comparison, not as a single correct answer.
In 2017, the Uttarakhand High Court declared the Ganga and Yamuna "living entities"; the Supreme Court later stayed that order, showing ongoing legal debate about the rights of nature.

vocabulary.meaning: human-centred view of value

examples: Whether a forest should be cleared for a mine raises all three views.
The 1984 Bhopal gas tragedy is a central case in environmental justice debates in India.

Each was reasoning from different values.

lessons.title: Design an Action Project
objectives: Explain key Indian environmental laws and institutions
Plan, run and evaluate a community environmental project
explanation: India's environmental framework includes the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, the Water Act 1974, the Air Act 1981, the Environment (Protection) Act 1986 and the National Green Tribunal (2010), which hears environmental cases. Article 48A of the Constitution directs the state to protect the environment, and Article 51A(g) makes it a fundamental duty of citizens.
Citizen science lets ordinary people collect real data — bird counts, air quality readings, river monitoring — that help researchers and decision-makers.

Effective projects start with a clear problem and baseline data, set measurable goals, involve stakeholders, act, then measure results honestly and share what was learned — including what didn't work.

story.title: The Data That Changed a Decision
story.text: Students noticed heavy traffic smoke outside their school. For three months they recorded air quality readings with a simple sensor and counted vehicles. They presented charts to the municipality. A no-idling zone and a new pedestrian crossing followed. "Our numbers," one student said, "were more convincing than our complaints."
